14.0.s.en: (1) Samson asks his parents to get him a Philistine girl as wife

14.0.0.en: Timnath: a city in the tribe of Judah, given to the tribe of Dan (Josh 15:10, 19:43), but the Philistines recovered it. It lies near the city of Zorah but at a level about 250 meters lower, because Zorah, the city of Samson and his parents, stands about 50 meters above sea level (map 12). Samson went down from Zorah to Timnath, inhabited by the Philistines, and took a liking to a Philistine girl there.

14.1.0.en: When he returned to Zorah he told his parents that he had seen in Timnath a Philistine woman who pleased him and that he wanted to marry her, and he asked them to betroth her to him as a wife. It is a tradition still followed in most societies that parents betroth wives for their sons.

14.2.0.en: "The uncircumcised Philistines": that is, those not circumcised. Circumcision was a symbol or sign of the covenant between God and His people (Gen 17:10, 11 - Deut 21:10); what is meant is the uncircumcised Philistine men, of whose people this girl was.

14.2.1.en: These steps were contrary to the law and to the Lord's warnings to His people not to mix with strangers and intermarry with them, lest they draw His people into pagan worship (Deut 7:3, 4). His devout parents knew what the law imposed, so they questioned him about his choice and proposed to him marriage to the daughters of his own kin, but he insisted on his request. Here the mastery of the desire for women over Samson appears, for when he took a liking to a pagan girl he broke the law and wanted to marry her, forgetting that he was a Nazarite of God, and the Nazarite today is equivalent to the consecrated servant, that is, one who holds fast to God's commandments with exactness.

14.2.2.en: Do not submit to your desires and so break God's commandments, especially at marriage, and neglect the guidance of your parents, for you will meet troubles you will be forced to bear all your life; rather let God be your guide through many prayers, in addition to the guidance of all who are loyal to you.

14.3.0.en: "But his father and his mother knew not that it was of the LORD": it was by the guidance of the Lord, to be the cause of fighting the Philistines.

14.3.1.en: His parents did not know that God, in His arrangement for the deliverance of the children of Israel by the hand of Samson, had allowed this situation in order to take vengeance on the Philistines who had humbled His people. This does not mean that God pushed him into the error, but He used his error to be the cause of disciplining the Philistines and requiting them, because the Philistines were dominating the children of Israel and harassing them. As the Scripture says, "All things work together for good to them that love God" (Rom 8:28). And this expression which the inspired writer used, "that it was of the LORD," means by God's permission to discipline the Philistines; so what Samson did was an error which God turned to the good of His people.

14.4.s.en: (2) The story of Samson's killing the lion

14.4.0.en: "The Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him": the Holy Spirit came upon him to give him courage and strength.

14.4.1.en: Samson's parents yielded to his request, on which he insisted, and went with him to Timnath, and passed through a place full of grapevines. Samson's steps were faster than his parents' steps, and behold a young lion met him on his way, and as soon as it saw Samson before it, it began to roar, ready to attack. Here divine providence intervened to give Samson strength and courage to seize the lion and rend it in two as though it were a small kid, and what Samson did was without a weapon in his hand. Samson did this without telling his parents what he had done, out of humility on his part and giving the credit to the One who deserves it, God, who grants strength.

14.5.0.en: They all reached Timnath and went forward to betroth the Philistine woman whom Samson had liked earlier from her appearance, and now his liking for her increased after he had talked with her. And after he betrothed her he returned with his parents to the city of Zorah.

14.6.0.en: "The carcase": the body of the lion and its skeleton.

14.6.1.en: "A swarm of bees": a group of bees making a hive.

14.6.2.en: They all returned to Zorah, and after several days they travelled again to Timnath - after the period of betrothal had ended - to complete the marriage. On their way toward Timnath Samson turned toward the place where he had wrestled with the lion to see what had become of the carcass of the lion, and its body had turned into a skeleton and had become a suitable place for bees to form a hive to make honey.

14.7.0.en: "He took thereof": he took from it.

14.7.1.en: Samson took some of the honey in his hands and ate of it, and carried some of it to his parents, and did not tell them that he had taken it from the mouth of the lion, perhaps so that they would not refrain from eating it because it was from the inside of a dead animal, which the law forbids.

14.7.2.en: The law forbade touching dead bodies, but the body may have decomposed and nothing remained but the skeleton, or it may have been a weakness in Samson that he was not exact in carrying out the law.

14.7.3.en: God is able to give you strength to face dangers however hard they are, and is able also to turn tribulation into a blessing, as Samson overcame the lion and even turned its bones into a beehive from whose honey Samson ate. So do not be disturbed by tribulations, but ask God's help and trust in His support.

14.8.0.en: They all reached Timnath to complete the marriage and stayed as guests with the woman's family, and Samson held a wedding feast, as is customary in all ages and even now.

14.9.0.en: According to the customs in force in those times, when the bride's family saw that Samson was preparing a wedding feast, they invited thirty Philistine young men to sit with him at his feast and rejoice with him.

14.10.0.en: "Sheets": the garment worn underneath, which may be short.

14.10.1.en: "Change of garments": a robe reaching to the feet and worn outside, which may be embroidered.

14.10.2.en: The time of the feast came, and it was customary for it to be seven days, and Samson proposed to the Philistine young men who sat with him that he would tell them a riddle; if they could solve it he would give them thirty shirts and thirty robes, and if they could not, they had to give him thirty shirts and thirty robes. The young men accepted the conditions Samson set both in case they arrived at the solution of the riddle and in case they did not. And they showed readiness to hear the riddle, thinking that it was one of the common riddles that would not be hard for them to solve.

14.11.0.en: Samson told them the riddle in a beautiful poetic form: that out of the eater (he means the lion) came forth meat (that is, food), and out of the strong (he means the carcass of the lion, which had become bones) came forth sweetness (he means honey). The Philistine young men thought for three days and could not solve the riddle.

14.12.0.en: "Have ye called us to take that we have? is it not so?": was your inviting us to the feast intended to rob us, by our presenting robes and shirts to you.

14.12.1.en: "Entice thy husband": use guile on him.

14.12.2.en: The Philistine young men resorted to trickery to reach the solution of the riddle, so they went to the bride, Samson's wife, and urged her to use guile on Samson so as to learn from him the solution of the riddle, and they threatened her that they would burn her and her father's house with fire if she did not learn from him the solution of the riddle and bring it to them. They were extremely angry, denouncing the idea that the purpose of their invitation to the wedding was to rob them and force them to present shirts and robes.

14.13.0.en: Samson's wife pressed him and began to beg him in every way and flatter him, and wept to move his heart, and accused him of not loving her, for how could he tell a riddle to the young men of her people without making her know the solution of the riddle? And Samson would tell her that he had not told anyone, not even his parents, the solution of the riddle, so how could she be angry that he did not tell her the solution?

14.14.0.en: "She told the riddle to the children of her people": she told the children of her people the solution of the riddle as Samson had told it to her.

14.14.1.en: Samson's wife was most insistent on knowing the solution of the riddle, for the alternative was the Philistine young men's carrying out their threat to burn her and her family. So she persisted in her begging and weeping until she spoiled for him the joy of the wedding, and the feast turned for him into a lamentation instead of joy, and she troubled him so much that in the end he was compelled to tell her the solution of the riddle, and all she did was pass the solution on to the sons of her people. This shows Samson's weakness before the tears of women, for the desire for women had gained mastery over his heart and abolished his reason.

14.15.0.en: "If ye had not plowed with my heifer, ye had not found out my riddle": the heifer is the female of the cow or the buffalo, which was used in pulling the plow, and what is meant by it here is his wife; this is a deliberate comparison, meaning that if they had not resorted to his wife and pressed her, they could not have solved the riddle.

14.15.1.en: When the Philistines learned the solution of the riddle before the seventh day ended, they went to Samson and told him the solution, meaning that there is nothing sweeter than honey and nothing stronger than a lion. Samson was enraged, telling them that had they not laughed at his wife and resorted to her to learn the riddle, and pressed her as with a plow until they drew out what was inside her, as the plow brings out of the earth what is in its depths, they could not have solved it.

14.16.0.en: "He slew thirty men of them, and took their spoil": he took their clothes as booty after killing them.

14.16.1.en: Here a new coming of the Holy Spirit upon Samson took place to give him courage and strength, and he went to Ashkelon, one of the coastal cities of the Philistines, lying north of Gaza, and there he killed thirty men and brought their garments to the thirty young men who had revealed the solution of the riddle, according to the agreed wager. And Samson was very angry because the Philistines had used guile on his wife and because his wife had told them the solution of the riddle, so he did not complete the days of rejoicing at the wedding and did not enjoy it, but left his wife and went back to his father's house in Zorah.

14.16.2.en: We notice that the strength that was with Samson came from the coming of the Spirit of the Lord upon him and not from his hair; rather his hair is a sign of his love, his vow and the consecration of his life to God, and therefore, because of his submission to God, the Spirit of the Lord works in him.

14.17.0.en: "His companion, whom he had used as his friend": one of Samson's acquaintances, who perhaps helped him in the arrangements for the wedding.

14.17.1.en: The bride's father thought that Samson's leaving his wife without completing the days of rejoicing and returning to his country meant that he hated her and no longer wanted her as a wife, so he gave her to his companion, and this was a rashness on the part of the bride's father that led to bad results that we shall learn of afterward. Samson's leaving his wife was because of his anger at her for exposing his riddle, and afterward he would return to her.

14.17.2.en: Do not be hasty in your judgments, but seek God in prayer and also the counsel of your father of confession and of those who are loyal to you, so that you do not err, especially in great decisions, for what comes out of your mouth may be hard to correct. Samson takes vengeance on the Philistines for giving his wife in marriage to another

15.0.s.en: (1) Samson's anger at his wife's marriage to another

15.0.0.en: "Visited his wife": he wanted to visit his wife.

15.0.1.en: After some time since leaving his wife and returning to his father's house, when the fierceness of his anger over the matter of the riddle had calmed, he decided to visit his wife, perhaps to be reconciled with her, and he took with him a kid as a gift, as was common in those days. This was in the days of the wheat harvest, that is, the days of spring.

15.1.0.en: Samson wanted to be alone with his wife in the room set apart for her, but her father prevented him and told him that she was no longer his wife, for when he left her in his anger and went away they thought that he no longer wanted her as a wife, and one of his companions had come forward asking for her hand and they had in fact given her to him in marriage. And wishing to appease Samson, her father proposed to him that he marry her younger sister, praising her as better than the first.

15.2.0.en: This matter again aroused Samson's anger greatly, and he told them that now there was no blame on him if he punished the Philistines for the wrong they had done him, for the error was not the father's alone but was shared by his people, who could have prevented the girl's father from this conduct.

15.3.0.en: "Firebrands": materials that can be kindled, such as cloth.

15.3.1.en: Jackal: an animal living in Palestine, in size between the wolf and the fox.

15.3.2.en: "Burnt up the shocks": the shocks are the heaps of grain found on the threshing floors, which are wide areas beside the fields.

15.3.3.en: Samson took three hundred animals called jackals, and tied every two tails together and tied firebrands to the tails and then kindled them and let them loose among the fields of the Philistines. The animals, their tails on fire, began to run in madness at speed and burned the heaps of grain, the grapevines, the olive orchards and all the crops.

15.4.0.en: "The Timnite": Samson's father-in-law, who was from the city of Timnath.

15.4.1.en: The Philistines asked one another who could have done this, and learned that it was Samson, and that he had done it because his father-in-law had given his wife to his companion. The Philistines were very enraged at Samson because he had caused them heavy losses, so they seized Samson's father-in-law and burned him and his daughter and all his house, in vengeance on their part and as a satisfaction to Samson so that he would cease harming them.

15.5.0.en: Samson's anger did not abate after the burning of the woman and her father, and he was not appeased, as the Philistines had intended by burning her, but threatened the Philistines with more acts of vengeance on them in keeping with the wrong they had done him, and after that he would cease from them.

15.6.0.en: "He smote them hip and thigh": that is, he achieved a great victory over them.

15.6.2.en: Etam: a Hebrew word meaning the lair of wild beasts; it lies east of Zorah at a distance of 4 km. Samson won a great victory over them and killed a great number of them, and it was a great slaughter, and then he went to hide in a cave.

15.6.3.en: Know that God is just and will punish you for your sins if you do not repent of them, and the punishment of sin is death, so hasten to repentance to obtain God's forgiveness and mercies.

15.7.s.en: (2) The Philistines try to seize Samson

15.7.0.en: "Went up": the Philistines dwell south of the tribe of Judah, so their going up means their moving northward. Lehi: a high place, so called after Samson's victory over the Philistines with the lehi of an ass, that is, the jawbone of an ass.

15.7.1.en: Large numbers of the Philistines entered the land of Judah and spread out in a place near Zorah - Samson's homeland - in order to seize him and take vengeance on him.

15.8.0.en: "Why are ye come up against us?": why have you entered our lands?

15.8.1.en: The men of Judah asked the Philistines the reason for their coming into their lands, since there was at present no reason to fight them, for they were subject to slavery and had not declared disobedience or risen against them or fought them. The Philistines answered that they had come to look for Samson in order to take vengeance on him because he had burned their farms and crops and killed great numbers of them.

15.9.0.en: The men of Judah knew the place where Samson was hiding, so three thousand men of them went to him at the rock of Etam and reproached him for provoking the Philistines, who dominated them and whom they were unable to face. His answer to them was that he had not begun evil toward them, but it was they who began to wrong him, so what he did to them was a repayment of the wrong they had done him.

15.10.0.en: The men of Judah wanted to guard against the evil of the Philistines, who were poised against them, by handing Samson over to them, and they told him what they intended to do, which was to seize him and deliver him bound to the Philistines. Samson agreed with them on condition that they themselves would not harm him or kill him, and he asked them to swear to that.

15.10.1.en: Perhaps the children of Israel felt that one, Samson, should die for the whole people exposed to the Philistines' attacks. By this they signify the Jewish nation, which delivered Christ to the Romans to die, not for the nation only but for the whole world, as Caiaphas the high priest prophesied (Jn 11:50).

15.11.0.en: "Two new cords": that is, in perfect firmness and strength.

15.11.1.en: They promised him that they would not kill him but would bind him with ropes and deliver him to the Philistines, and then they bound him with two new cords and brought him out of the cave to deliver him into the enemies' hand.

15.11.2.en: Do not let fear move you to betray God and wrong His servants, as the tribe of Judah did by handing Samson over, but when fear fights you, ask God's help, and He will protect you and the servants of God.

15.12.s.en: (3) Samson kills a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of an ass

15.12.0.en: They brought him, bound with the ropes, to the town of Lehi, where the Philistines were waiting, and as soon as they saw him they raised their voices in exultation as they advanced toward him to get at him. And once again God gave him mighty strength, and he broke the strong ropes with which he was bound, which before his strength became a frail, weak thing like burnt flax.

15.13.0.en: "The jawbone of an ass": the jaw of an ass.

15.13.1.en: Samson had no weapon of any kind in his hand, but he looked around him and found the jaw of an ass that had recently died, a fresh, supple jaw that does not break easily as a dry one does, so he seized it and struck the Philistines with it and killed a thousand men of them, and the rest fled.

15.14.0.en: "With the jawbone of an ass, heaps upon heaps": he heaped their bodies in heaps with the jawbone of an ass.

15.14.1.en: Samson looked at the corpses piled on one another and began to say that with the jaw of an ass he had turned the enemy into heaps of slain: he had killed a thousand men and heaped them in two heaps.

15.15.0.en: The words that Samson said were like a song of victory, and as soon as he finished chanting them he cast the jaw of the ass from his hand and called the place where he threw it "Ramath-lehi," which in the Hebrew language means the place where the jaw was cast, as expressed in Arabic.

15.16.0.en: Samson was tired from striking the Philistines and exhausted from wrestling with them, and he became extremely thirsty, until he felt he was nearly dying of his thirst. So he turned to the Lord and prayed to Him, saying: You have wrought by my hand this great victory, and this is a confession from Samson that the strength is from God and not from himself, so will You be content that I die now of thirst and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised, that is, the uncircumcised Philistines?

15.17.0.en: "God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw": the hollow is a concave spot in the ground, that is, a pit, from which God brought out much water by a divine miracle.

15.17.1.en: En-hakkore: a Hebrew word meaning "the spring of the one who called," since Samson called upon the Lord in this place when he was thirsty (map 12). Since Samson had confessed that the victory achieved was from God, God answered his prayer and brought forth water for him from a dry spring, which is a spring of water that dries up in the summer season; God made water in it at a time when there was none. Samson drank and his spirit revived after he had almost died of thirst. And as a memorial of God's answering his prayer, the place was called En-hakkore, and the spring became a permanently flowing spring until the time the book was written.

15.18.0.en: Samson judged Israel in the days when the Philistines were dominating the children of Israel, and the length of his judging was twenty years; and although he did not deliver his people with a decisive deliverance, he was a source of fear and anxiety to their enemies and so broke the sharpness of their tyranny over his people.

15.18.1.en: As long as God is with you, do not be disturbed by the power of demons or of your enemies however many they are, and do not fear them however weak your means, for God is your strength and your victory.
